findings.finding: revision_history is not monotone and its labels are not self-consistent: index 8 is labelled rev11 and stamped 2026-09-11T23:32:53+08:00 with unused: true, index 9 is labelled rev3 and stamped 2026-09-11T23:30:35+08:00 with unused: true, both earlier than index 7 (rev10, 2026-09-12T00:30:00+08:00) and index 10 (rev12, 2026-09-12T00:31:41+08:00); there is no rev8 entry; revision: 12 with 10 entries of which 2 are flagged unused. A consumer that reads the last entry or the maximum timestamp gets rev12, but a consumer that reads the list in order sees revision numbers run 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,11,3,12. The artifact itself remains unambiguous (revision: 12 plus the rev12 delta text), so this is a machine-readability defect rather than a semantic one.
findings.falsifier: Show a documented ordering rule under which the list is monotone (none is stated in the artifact), or replace the block with a monotone history keyed by revision.

findings.finding: quantifiers.ordered binds (Sigma,h,K) to domain_id D2, whose definition is the data class, while quantifiers.formal, conclusion.statement_formal and quantifiers.order_note restrict the binder to G_r (a comeager subset of D2). A consumer of ordered[] alone would read the forbidden for-all-data strengthening. The same convention is used verbatim by F2a and F2b (ordered data binder -> D2, restriction only in formal), and the canonical structural gate (R03/R27) passes, so this is a shared representational risk rather than an F1-local divergence.
findings.falsifier: Show that no consumer reconstructs semantics from ordered[] alone (e.g. document that formal/statement_formal is authoritative), or add an explicit restriction field to the data rung.
